questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: state what a pair of parameter equations describes
questions.stem: A trolley moves so that its coordinates are x = 4t and y = 2t, with t in seconds. What does the ordered pair (x, y) record at each value of t?

options.text: The position of the trolley at that instant, in metres
The velocity of the trolley at that instant, in metres per second
options.misconception: reads the coordinate pair as a rate of change rather than a location

options.text: The total distance the trolley has already covered, in metres
options.misconception: reads the coordinate pair as an accumulated distance rather than a location

options.text: The compass bearing of the trolley, given as a direction rather than a place
options.misconception: reads the coordinate pair as a direction rather than a location

questions.explanation: The parameter t is an independent variable, and x and y are both functions of it, so each t produces exactly one point on the plane. That point is where the object is at that instant, which is why the pair is called a position. Differentiating x and y with respect to t would give the velocity, and the coordinates themselves say nothing about how far the object has travelled along a winding path, nor do they name a bearing without a stated origin and frame.
questions.hint: Ask what happens at t = 0: does the pair give a place or a rate?

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: eliminate a parameter and use the interval that survives
questions.stem: A point is traced by x = 2t + 1 and y = 4t - 6 as t runs from 0 to 3. What is the largest value of y reached along that traced segment? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Solving x = 2t + 1 for t gives t = (x - 1)/2, and substituting that into y = 4t - 6 turns the path into the straight line y = 2x - 8. Keeping the parameter interval is what makes the answer finite: t between 0 and 3 means x between 1 and 7, so y = 2x - 8 only runs from -6 up to 6. Reporting -6 uses the wrong end of the segment, and 14 comes from letting t keep growing past 3, which forgets that the tracer never goes there.
questions.hint: Eliminate t first, then translate the parameter interval into a range for x.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain what an eliminated parameter fails to record
questions.stem: A marker moves along x = 3 cos t and y = 3 sin t for 0 at most t at most pi. Once t is eliminated the equation is x squared plus y squared equals 9. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The equation together with the condition that y is at least zero traces exactly the traced path
The equation on its own traces exactly the same set of points as the parameter range
options.misconception: assumes eliminating the parameter loses no information about the range of angles

options.text: The equation together with the condition that x is at least zero traces exactly the traced path
options.misconception: confuses the half of the circle that is traced with the wrong quadrant condition

options.text: The equation together with the condition that y is at most zero traces exactly the traced path
options.misconception: picks the lower semicircle when the parameter range traces the upper one

questions.explanation: For t between 0 and pi the sine of t is never negative, so y never drops below the x axis and only the upper semicircle is walked; x itself runs from 3 down to -3, so no condition on x is needed. The eliminated equation forgets the parameter range entirely and by itself draws the whole circle. That is the general trap: elimination can add points, because the resulting equation admits every solution, not only the ones a real t can produce.
questions.hint: Check the sign of the sine over the stated parameter range before eliminating it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the slope of a parametric curve by differentiation
questions.stem: For the curve x = t squared minus 4 and y = t cubed minus 3t, what is the slope dy over dx at the parameter value t = 2?

options.misconception: inverts the quotient and returns the horizontal rate over the vertical rate
halves the horizontal rate, as if dx over dt were t rather than 2t
inverts the quotient and also halves the horizontal rate

questions.explanation: Differentiate each coordinate with respect to the parameter: dx/dt is 2t and dy/dt is 3t squared minus 3. At t = 2 the horizontal rate is 4 and the vertical rate is 9, and the slope of the traced path is the quotient of the vertical rate by the horizontal rate, so 9 over 4. The reversed quotient 4 over 9 belongs to dx/dy, which is the reciprocal slope and answers a different question, and dividing by t instead of 2t quietly drops a factor of two.
questions.hint: Write both coordinate rates with respect to t, then take vertical over horizontal.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: locate horizontal tangents from a parametric derivative
questions.stem: A curve is traced by x = t squared minus 1 and y = t cubed minus 3t. How many horizontal tangent lines does it carry, and which two points do they touch?

options.text: Two of them, meeting the curve at the point where x is 0 and y is 2 and at the point where x is 0 and y is -2
Two of them, meeting the curve at the point where x is -1 and y is 0 and at the point where x is 0 and y is 3
options.misconception: reads the zeros of the horizontal rate as zeros of the vertical rate

options.text: One of them, meeting the curve at the point where x is 0 and y is 0
options.misconception: looks only for a parameter value where both coordinate rates vanish at once

options.text: Two of them, meeting the curve at the point where x is 1 and y is 0 and at the point where x is 0 and y is 1
options.misconception: picks parameter values from the wrong roots of the vertical rate

questions.explanation: A horizontal tangent needs the vertical rate to be zero while the horizontal rate is not, since the slope is the vertical rate divided by the horizontal one. Here dy/dt is 3t squared minus 3, which vanishes at t = 1 and t = -1, and at both of those values dx/dt is 2t, equal to 2 and -2, so neither tangent is vertical and the slope really is zero. Substituting gives x = 0 at both values with y equal to -2 at t = 1 and y equal to 2 at t = -1.
questions.hint: Set the vertical rate to zero, then confirm the horizontal rate is not zero there.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain what a vanishing velocity vector does to a curve
questions.stem: Both coordinate rates of the path x = t cubed and y = t to the fourth vanish when t = 0. Which reading of that instant is correct?

options.text: The velocity vector is the zero vector at that instant, yet the path runs smoothly through the point with a horizontal tangent
The curve halts at that point, because a zero velocity means the tracing stops there
options.misconception: reads a zero velocity vector as the end of the path rather than an instant of rest

options.text: The curve has a sharp corner at that point, because two vanishing rates cannot agree
options.misconception: assumes vanishing coordinate rates always produce a corner instead of a smooth turning tangent

options.text: The curve is undefined at that point, because a zero over zero slope is not a number
options.misconception: treats an undefined slope quotient as a missing point on the curve

questions.explanation: A zero velocity vector means the object is momentarily at rest, not that the path has ended: the same point is reached again for parameter values just past and just before the instant. Dividing the two coordinate rates before simplifying gives 4t over 3, which tends to 0, so the tangent line at the origin is horizontal and the curve passes through smoothly as y equal to the absolute value of x to the four thirds power. A cusp or a genuine corner needs one-sided slopes that disagree, and an undefined slope is normal at a vertical tangent.
questions.hint: Simplify the slope quotient before deciding what happens at the point.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute speed from parametric coordinate rates
questions.stem: A drone flies along the path x = 4t cubed and y = 3t to the fourth. What is its speed, in units per second, at the instant t = 1? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The velocity vector has components 12t squared and 12t cubed, which at t = 1 are both 12, and the speed is the magnitude of that vector, the square root of 12 squared plus 12 squared, that is 12 times the square root of 2, about 16.9706. Adding the two components to get 24 confuses a vector with a scalar sum, and squaring instead of taking a square root leaves an area. The two equal components are a coincidence of the chosen instant, not a general rule.
questions.hint: Differentiate both coordinates, then take the square root of the sum of the squares.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a second derivative from a parametric curve
questions.stem: A curve is traced by x = 2t cubed and y = 9t to the fourth. What is the value of the second derivative of y with respect to x when t = 1? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Differentiate twice: the horizontal rate is 6t squared, the vertical rate is 36t cubed, the vertical second derivative is 108t squared and the horizontal second derivative is 12t. The second derivative with respect to x is the vertical rate times the horizontal second derivative minus the vertical second derivative times the horizontal rate, all over the cube of the horizontal rate. At t = 1 that is (648 - 432) over 216, which is 1.
questions.hint: Apply the second derivative formula that combines the four first and second coordinate rates.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Tangent line to a parametric curve
questions.learningObjective: write the tangent line at a given parameter value
questions.stem: A curve is traced by x = t squared and y = 3t. Which equation gives the tangent line at the parameter value t = 2?

options.misconception: uses the reciprocal of the slope and then forces the line through the point
uses the y coordinate of the point as though it were the vertical intercept
gets the slope right but subtracts the point offset instead of adding it

questions.explanation: At t = 2 the curve is at the point whose coordinates are 4 and 6, and the slope there is the vertical rate 3 over the horizontal rate 2t, which is 4, so the slope is 3/4. Substituting the point into y minus 6 equals 3/4 of x minus 4 gives y equal to 3x/4 plus 3, and substituting x = 4 returns 6 as it must. The reciprocal slope 4/3 still passes through the point but leans the wrong way, and reading the y coordinate as the intercept forgets the horizontal offset.
questions.hint: Compute the point and the slope at t = 2, then use point-slope form and simplify.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: describe the set of points a parameter range produces
questions.stem: As t runs from 0 to 1, a point traces x = 2t and y = 2t squared. Which set of points is actually reached?

options.text: The part of the parabola y = x squared over 2 with x running from 0 to 2
The whole parabola y = x squared over 2, with no restriction on x
options.misconception: drops the parameter interval and treats the eliminated equation as the whole path

options.text: The part of the parabola y = x squared over 2 with y running from 0 to 2
options.misconception: puts the parameter interval on the wrong coordinate of the pair

options.text: The part of the parabola y = x squared over 2 with x running from -2 to 2
options.misconception: assumes a parameter of this form must sweep both signs of t

questions.explanation: From x = 2t the parameter is t = x/2, and substituting into y = 2t squared gives y = x squared over 2, but the range 0 to 1 for t becomes a range of 0 to 2 for x. So the traced set is a single arc of the parabola, not the whole curve. The parameter interval always has to be carried along, and it belongs on whichever coordinate the interval was given for, so the arc is limited in x, not in y.
questions.hint: Solve for the parameter, substitute, and then translate the parameter interval into a coordinate range.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: locate an extreme coordinate value on a parameter interval
questions.stem: A mark moves along x = 3t - t squared and y = t squared while t runs from 0 to 2. What is the largest horizontal coordinate it reaches? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The horizontal coordinate is a concave-down quadratic in t, so its largest value on a closed interval is found where dx/dt vanishes, at 3 - 2t = 0, giving t = 3/2, which does lie inside the interval. Substituting gives 3 times 3/2 minus 9/4, that is 9/2 - 9/4 = 9/4 = 2.25. Checking only the endpoints would find the value 2 at t = 2 and miss the interior maximum, and a negative sign on the squared term would flip the vertex into a minimum.
questions.hint: Find where the horizontal rate is zero, confirm that value is inside the interval, then substitute.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute speed from parametric coordinate rates
questions.stem: A courier travels along x = 5t and y = 2t squared, with t in seconds. Which value is the courier's speed at t = 3?

options.misconception: adds the two coordinate rates instead of taking the magnitude of the velocity vector
multiplies the two coordinate rates, which has the units of a rate squared
subtracts the smaller coordinate rate from the larger instead of combining them in quadrature

questions.explanation: The coordinate rates are 5 and 4t, so at t = 3 the velocity vector is <5, 12> and the speed is the magnitude of that vector, the square root of 25 + 144, which is 13. That is the familiar right-triangle shape of a 5 by 12 by 13 triple. Adding the components to get 17 treats a vector sum as a distance, and the product 60 has units of a different kind altogether, being a rate multiplied by a rate.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the sum of the squares of the two coordinate rates.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compare how sharply two curves bend
questions.stem: A robot arm swings along a circular arc of radius 4 centimetres, and a second arm swings along a circular arc of radius 2 centimetres. What distinguishes the two paths?

options.text: The radius-2 path bends more sharply, since it turns through the same angle over half as much arc length
The radius-4 path bends more sharply, since a longer radius sweeps more turning per unit length
options.misconception: believes a longer radius produces more turning per unit of arc length

options.text: Both paths bend equally, since a circle is a circle whatever its radius
options.misconception: assumes every circle carries the same amount of bending per unit length

options.text: Nothing distinguishes them, since curvature measures the speed of the mechanism rather than the shape
options.misconception: confuses the curvature of the path with the rate at which the mechanism moves

questions.explanation: Curvature measures how much the direction of travel turns per unit of distance travelled, so a tight circle accumulates turning faster than a wide one over the same length of path. Over an arc of a fixed length the smaller radius sweeps a larger angle, which is why the radius-2 arm has the larger curvature, here 1/2 against 1/4. Curvature is purely geometric and has nothing to do with how quickly either arm is driven.
questions.hint: Fix a length of path and compare how much the direction of travel turns over it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: state the curvature of a path that never turns
questions.stem: A trolley rolls along a straight track and its speed is changing from second to second. What can be concluded about the curvature of the path it follows?

options.text: The curvature of the path is zero, because the direction of travel never changes
The curvature is undefined, because a straight line has no natural length to measure
options.misconception: believes curvature is undefined whenever a path has no turning at all

options.text: The curvature equals the speed, so a faster trolley follows a curvier path
options.misconception: confuses the rate of travel along the path with the rate at which the path turns

options.text: The curvature is infinite, since a straight line has an infinitely large radius of turn
options.misconception: confuses the radius of the turning circle with the curvature itself

questions.explanation: Curvature is the rate of change of the direction of travel with respect to distance travelled, so if the direction is constant the curvature is exactly zero however fast the trolley moves. Speed along the path and turning of the path are different things, which is why an accelerating trolley on a straight track still has zero curvature. Zero curvature corresponds to an infinitely large radius of turn, so the last wording has the number right and the name of the quantity wrong.
questions.hint: Ask whether the direction of travel changes as the trolley covers distance.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute the curvature of a graph at a point
questions.stem: A track follows the parabola y = 3x squared. What is the curvature of the track at the point where x = 0? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The curvature of a graph is the magnitude of its second derivative divided by one plus the square of its first derivative, all raised to the three halves. For y = 3x squared the first derivative is 6x and the second derivative is 6, so at x = 0 the curvature is 6 divided by 1 to the three halves, which is 6. The radius of the turning circle there is the reciprocal, 1/6, and reporting that instead confuses curvature with the radius of the osculating circle.
questions.hint: Differentiate twice, then divide the magnitude of the second derivative by the usual power of one plus the slope squared.

questions.learningObjective: state the curvature of a circle from its radius
questions.stem: A path is the circle x squared plus y squared equals 25. What is the curvature of that path at the point (5, 0)? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The curvature of a circle is the reciprocal of its radius, and the same value holds at every point because a circle turns at a constant rate. The equation shows the radius is 5, so the curvature is 1 over 5, that is 0.2. Taking 25 as the input instead of 5 confuses the squared radius on the left of the equation with the radius itself, and quoting the radius answers a different question about the same circle.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute speed from parametric coordinate rates
questions.stem: A particle follows the path x = t cubed and y = t squared plus 3t. What is its speed at t = 1? Report the number only.

The sum 8 is a scalar combination of the components and is not a distance, the difference 2 is not a distance either, and taking the components in the opposite order answers a question about dy/dx rather than about how fast the particle moves.

questions.learningObjective: recover the polar radius from Cartesian coordinates
questions.stem: A monitoring station sits at the Cartesian point (-6, 8), with both numbers in kilometres. What is its polar radius from the origin? Report the number only.

A radius is a distance and so cannot come out negative, and the point lies in the second quadrant, which fixes the angle but leaves this length untouched. Adding the coordinates to get 2 measures a broken path rather than a straight one.
questions.hint: Square both coordinates, add them, and take the positive square root.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: convert a polar point to a Cartesian coordinate
questions.stem: A target is described in polar coordinates by r = 12 and an angle of 5pi over 6. What is its vertical coordinate? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The vertical coordinate of a polar point is r times the sine of its angle, and the sine of 5pi over 6 is one half because that angle sits in the second quadrant, where sine stays positive. Multiplying gives 12 times one half, that is 6. Using the sine of the reference angle pi over 6 gives the same number here only by luck, because the sine happens to be symmetric about pi over 2, whereas the cosine does not behave that way and does come out negative.
questions.hint: The vertical coordinate is r times the sine of the angle; check the quadrant sign first.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute the total area of a rose curve
questions.stem: A decorative inlay fills the region traced by r = 4 cos 3 theta, taking in all three petals. What is its total area? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The area of a polar region is one half the integral of r squared, so here it is one half the integral from 0 to 2pi of 16 cos squared of 3 theta, and the integral of a cosine squared over a full turn is pi whatever its frequency. That gives one half of 16 pi, which is 8 pi, about 25.1327. Running the integral only from 0 to pi would find just two of the three petals, and omitting the half would report twice the true area.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a polar arc length
questions.stem: A rail link follows the polar curve r = 2 cos theta from the point (2, 0) to the origin, that is for theta running from 0 to pi over 2. What is the length of that arc? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The polar arc length is the integral of the square root of r squared plus the square of the radius derivative, and here the two pieces are 4 cos squared theta and 4 sin squared theta, whose sum is 4. The integrand is therefore the constant 2, and the integral from 0 to pi over 2 is pi, about 3.1416. Geometrically the curve is the circle of radius 1 centred one unit along the positive x axis, and the arc in question is half of it, whose length is pi.
questions.hint: Combine r squared and its derivative squared before integrating; the sum may be constant.

questions.learningObjective: compute the area enclosed by a limaçon

The first two pieces integrate to 8pi and zero because the cosine integrates to nothing over a full turn, and the last integrates to pi. So the area is one half of 9pi, that is 9pi over 2, about 14.1372. Dropping the factor of one half doubles the answer to 9pi.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Where the polar area factor comes from
questions.learningObjective: justify the extra factor in the polar area formula
questions.stem: Explain why the area of a region bounded by a polar curve is written as one half the integral of the square of the radius, and say what the one half stands for.

answer.exemplar: A region under a polar curve is built from thin wedges, not thin strips. Take the wedge between the angles theta and theta plus d theta at radius r: the two straight sides have length r and the angle between them is d theta, so the wedge has area one half r squared d theta. Adding up consecutive wedges replaces the sum by the integral of that expression, which is one half the integral of r squared with respect to theta. The one half is therefore the area of a triangle, and it appears because the wedge is triangular rather than rectangular. A student who expects a rectangle here is really expecting a Cartesian strip, and a strip of unit width at radius r does not stay a unit wide once it is bent around the origin.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to make the geometric origin of the one half visible, because the factor is usually quoted without it and the resulting integral is then doubled or halved at random.
questions.hint: Compare a thin wedge of the region with a thin Cartesian strip, and see which shape the region is actually made of.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the information an eliminated parameter loses
questions.stem: Explain why eliminating a parameter from a pair of equations can describe a larger set of points than the original parameter range traces, and say what must be added back.

answer.exemplar: Elimination works by finding an equation that every traced point satisfies, and it is a one-way step: the traced points form a subset of the solutions of the new equation, not the other way round. The parameter range is what restricts the subset, and once t is gone nothing in the remaining equation records it. A quarter turn of a circle gives x squared plus y squared equal to 1, whose solutions run all the way round, so the eliminated equation adds a lower semicircle the tracer never visits. What has to be added back is a condition on the coordinates, such as both being non-negative, that the parameter range would have enforced. This is the same situation as squaring both sides of an equation and keeping only the solutions that can be traced back to a real parameter.

questions.explanation: The exemplar stresses that elimination loses a restriction rather than gaining a wrong equation, and names the type of extra condition that repairs it.
questions.hint: Think about which direction the reasoning runs, and about what the parameter range was doing that the equation cannot.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why a zero velocity does not end a path
questions.stem: Explain why a particle whose velocity vector is the zero vector at one instant is still travelling along a curve that continues past that point.

answer.exemplar: A zero velocity vector at one instant says the particle is momentarily at rest, not that it has left the path. Velocity is a derivative, and a derivative vanishing at a point constrains only that point, exactly as the derivative of x squared is zero at the origin although the line continues on both sides. For the path x = t cubed with y = t to the fourth, both coordinate rates vanish at t = 0, yet the same point is reached again for parameter values just above and just below 0, and the slope 4t over 3 tends to 0, so the tangent there is horizontal. The correct reading is an instant of rest on a smooth path, whereas a path that genuinely stopped would need the parameter range to end at that value.

questions.explanation: The exemplar rules out the reading that a vanishing derivative halts the curve, since derivatives vanish at ordinary points all the time.
questions.hint: Compare with the derivative of a simple polynomial at its turning point.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why speed is the length of the velocity vector
questions.stem: Explain why the speed of a particle is the magnitude of its velocity vector rather than the sum of the coordinate rates.

answer.exemplar: In a second coordinate unit the two coordinate rates are the horizontal and vertical legs of a right triangle, and the distance covered in a small interval of time is the hypotenuse, by the Pythagorean theorem. Speed is that distance divided by the interval of time, so speed equals the square root of the sum of the squares of the two rates, which is precisely the magnitude of the velocity vector. Adding the two rates instead would measure the length of the broken path that goes along the horizontal leg and then along the vertical one, which is longer than the straight-line distance actually travelled. The rule generalises to three dimensions in exactly the same way, and it is the same reason that a displacement vector is combined by magnitude and not by summing its components.

questions.explanation: The exemplar ties the formula to a right triangle, which is the reason the components combine in quadrature instead of by addition.
questions.hint: Draw the displacement over a small time interval and look at the shape it makes.

options.text: The vector <2x, -3>, which depends on the horizontal position but is constant in the vertical direction
The vector <x, 3y>, which grows in both coordinates as the position moves
options.misconception: believes the exponent carries over when differentiating and the sign of the term flips too

options.text: The vector <2x, 3>, which is constant in the horizontal and vertical directions alike
options.misconception: believes differentiating with respect to y keeps the exponent and loses the minus sign

options.text: The vector <2x, -3y>, which mixes the two coordinates in a way no graph shows
options.misconception: believes the partial derivative with respect to y must still involve y

questions.explanation: Differentiating with respect to x gives 2x and differentiating with respect to y gives -3, so the gradient is <2x, -3>. The vertical component is constant because a term in y alone differentiates to a fixed number, with no y left over, and the minus sign is carried through the derivative unchanged. The sign error in the second option is the commonest one here, since the derivative of -3y with respect to y is -3 and not +3.
questions.hint: Differentiate each term with respect to one coordinate while holding the other fixed.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: read the divergence of a simple vector field
questions.stem: A two-dimensional field is F of x comma y equal to <2x, 3y>. What does the divergence of this field equal, and what does that value say?

options.text: It equals 5 everywhere, so every small box has net outward flow of 5 per unit area
It equals 0 everywhere, so there is no net flow through any small box
options.misconception: believes a field whose components both grow must still have zero net flow

options.text: It equals 5 everywhere, so every small box has net inward flow of 5 per unit area
options.misconception: confuses the sign of a positive divergence, which is outward rather than inward

options.text: It equals x plus y, so the flow is strong along one diagonal and weak along the other
options.misconception: adds the two components together instead of differentiating each one

questions.explanation: The divergence is the sum of the partial derivatives of the components, so it is 2 + 3 = 5, a constant. A positive divergence means a small region around any point loses more fluid through its boundary than it gains, that is there is a net source. Neither component has to be negative for that to happen: each is growing with distance in its own direction, so the field is expanding everywhere, which is exactly what a positive divergence records.
questions.hint: Differentiate each component with respect to its own coordinate and add, then read the sign.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: state the gradient of a constant function
questions.stem: A height field over a flat region is described by the constant function f of x comma y equal to 7. What is the gradient of that function?

options.text: The zero vector, since the height does not increase in any direction
The vector <7, 0>, since the value of the function becomes a component
options.misconception: believes the value of a constant function becomes a component of its gradient

options.text: The vector <1, 1>, since every direction counts as an increase
options.misconception: believes a positive constant must increase along every direction

options.text: The vector <7, 7>, since both coordinates carry the constant value
options.misconception: believes each coordinate of the gradient equals the constant

questions.explanation: Differentiating a constant with respect to any coordinate gives zero, so every component of the gradient is zero and the gradient is the zero vector. That is the correct reading of a flat field: there is no direction of steepest increase, because no direction increases at all. The value 7 is the height itself, and it is not a rate, so it has no place in a gradient whose components are all rates of change per unit distance.
questions.hint: Differentiate a constant with respect to a coordinate and see what comes out.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: interpret the magnitude of a vector
questions.stem: A survey drone reports a displacement of <2, -5, 1> in kilometres. What is that magnitude reporting about the flight?

options.text: The straight-line distance from the starting point to the ending point
The total path length flown, which is longer whenever the flight turns
options.misconception: confuses the straight-line distance with the length of the actual route

options.text: The component of the flight along the third coordinate axis alone
options.misconception: reads a single coordinate as though it were the whole magnitude

options.text: The rate at which the position changes, in kilometres per hour
options.misconception: confuses a displacement, which is a position difference, with a velocity

questions.explanation: The magnitude of a displacement vector is the length of the straight segment joining the two positions, so it measures how far apart start and finish are and not how far the drone actually travelled. Those two agree only for a straight flight with no reversals, and on any curved route the flown distance is longer. Magnitude is also a length rather than a rate, which is why the last wording does not fit a vector whose components are quoted in kilometres.
questions.hint: Picture the displacement as the closing side of the triangle traced by the flight.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the slope of a polar curve at an angle
questions.stem: A path is drawn by the polar rule r = 2 sin 3 theta. What is the slope of that path at the angle theta = pi over 6?

options.misconception: drops the minus sign contributed by the denominator
believes a vanishing radius derivative means the path has no slope there
divides by the radius alone instead of by the whole denominator

questions.explanation: The polar slope rule puts the radius derivative times the sine plus the radius times the cosine over the radius derivative times the cosine minus the radius times the sine, and here the radius is 2 and the radius derivative is 6 cos 3 theta. At theta = pi over 6 the radius derivative vanishes, so the numerator reduces to the radius times the cosine of the angle, which is 2 times the cosine of pi over 6, that is the square root of 3, and the denominator reduces to minus the radius times the sine of the angle, which is -1. The slope is therefore minus the square root of 3, about -1.7321. A vanishing radius derivative does not make the slope zero, because the radius itself is still turning and contributes the r cos theta and r sin theta pieces; two independent checks agree, since the same point on the curve gives the same slope whether the curve is treated parametrically or converted to an implicit Cartesian equation and differentiated.
questions.hint: Substitute the angle and simplify the numerator and denominator separately before dividing.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: build a velocity vector from a parametric rule
questions.stem: A trolley is driven along the path x = 2t and y = 3t squared, with t in seconds. Which ordered pair gives its velocity at t = 2?

options.misconception: reports the position at that instant instead of differentiating it
differentiates the horizontal rule but leaves the vertical one alone
differentiates the vertical rule correctly but reports the horizontal rate as the t coefficient

questions.explanation: Differentiating x = 2t with respect to t gives 2, and differentiating y = 3t squared gives 6t, which at t = 2 is 12, so the velocity is <4, 12>. The pair <2, 6> is the position at that instant, not a rate, and it is easy to confuse the two when the numbers are small. The other two options each differentiate one rule and leave the other in its original form.
questions.hint: Differentiate both rules with respect to the parameter before substituting.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Area of a single rose petal
questions.learningObjective: compute the area of one petal of a rose curve
questions.stem: A flower shape is drawn by r = 2 sin 3 theta. What is the area of a single petal of that shape? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The first petal is painted as the radius grows from 0 up to its maximum, which happens at 3 theta = pi over 2, that is theta = pi over 6, and the petal closes when the radius returns to 0 at 3 theta = pi, that is theta = pi over 3. Over that range the area is one half the integral of 4 sin squared 3 theta, and sin squared has average one half over any whole number of half-periods, which here is one and a half periods, giving 4 pi over 12, that is pi over 3, about 1.0472. Integrating over 0 to 2pi would give all three petals, three times too much.
questions.hint: Find the angles where the radius is zero and where it is largest, and integrate between them.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Area of a washer-shaped polar region
questions.learningObjective: compute the area of a washer-shaped polar region and pick the right angular range
questions.stem: A washer-shaped plate lies inside the circle r = 2 cos theta and outside the circle r = 1. What is the area of the plate? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The rule r = 2 cos theta draws the circle of radius 1 centred one unit along the positive horizontal axis, and the two circles cross where 2 cos theta = 1, that is at theta = pi over 3 and again at 5pi over 3. The plate is where 2 cos theta is the larger radius, and that only happens on the two short arcs from 0 to pi over 3 and from 5pi over 3 to 2pi, not on the long arc between the crossings where the roles swap. By symmetry the two pieces are equal, so the area is the integral of 4 cos squared theta minus 1 from 0 to pi over 3, which works out to pi over 3 plus the square root of 3 over 2, about 1.9132. The geometry agrees: the plate is the whole shifted disc of area pi minus the lens where the two unit discs overlap, and that lens has area 2 pi over 3 minus the square root of 3 over 2, giving the same 1.9132. Integrating over the long arc instead returns 1.2284, which is the lens rather than the plate.
questions.hint: Find the crossing angles, then check on which arcs the 2 cos theta radius is actually the larger of the two.
